title: Chapter 5: Inflation and Deflation
benchmark: Paul Krugman & Robin Wells, Macroeconomics (Principles SSOT, Spring 2027)

questions.topic: Consumer Price Index vs. GDP Implicit Price Deflator Scope
questions.title: Consumer Price Index vs. GDP Implicit Price Deflator Scope
questions.prompt_template: How does the Consumer Price Index (CPI) differ from the GDP Implicit Price Deflator in the goods and services it covers?

hints.text: Recall which index tracks purchases by typical urban households and which index tracks domestic final production (C, I, G, X).
Think about how a foreign-made car or imported olive oil bought by a U.S. consumer is treated in each index.

options_template.text: The CPI tracks a fixed basket of urban consumer purchases including imported consumer goods, whereas the GDP Deflator covers all domestically produced final goods and services with changing weights.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The CPI measures retail prices paid by urban consumers (including imports), while the GDP Deflator measures prices across all domestic final output (C, I, G, X) and excludes imports.

options_template.text: The CPI covers all domestically produced capital and military goods, whereas the GDP Deflator covers only imported consumer groceries and apparel.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Scope): Capital equipment and government defense purchases enter the GDP Deflator, while imported consumer goods enter the CPI.

options_template.text: The CPI updates its basket quantities every quarter, whereas the GDP Deflator holds base-year quantities permanently fixed.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Weighting Structure): The standard CPI uses fixed short-run base-period basket weights (Laspeyres), whereas the GDP Deflator uses current-period changing quantities.

options_template.text: Both indexes cover the exact same basket of domestic goods, differing only because the CPI uses a base value of 1,000 while the GDP Deflator uses 100.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Base Normalization): Both indexes normalize the base period to 100, and their underlying baskets differ substantially in import coverage and weighting.

questions.topic: Distinguishing Disinflation from Deflation
questions.title: Distinguishing Disinflation from Deflation
questions.prompt_template: If an economy's annual CPI inflation rate falls from 6.0% last year to 2.5% this year, the economy is experiencing:

hints.text: Check whether the inflation rate is positive or negative this year.
Ask whether the aggregate price level is falling outright or still rising at a slower rate.

options_template.text: Disinflation, because the aggregate price level is still rising (+2.5%), just at a slower pace than last year.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Disinflation occurs whenever the inflation rate decreases toward zero while remaining strictly positive.

options_template.text: Deflation, because a lower inflation rate means average retail prices dropped by 3.5%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Confusing Disinflation with Deflation): Average prices only fall when the inflation rate turns negative; at +2.5%, prices still rose 2.5% over the year.

options_template.text: Zero inflation, because the price level stabilized back at its base-year value of 100.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Price Level vs. Rate of Change): A slowdown in inflation from 6.0% to 2.5% adds another 2.5% onto last year's elevated price level.

options_template.text: Hyperinflation, because cumulative prices rose by 8.5% across the two-year period.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Scale of Inflation): Moderate single-digit inflation is nowhere near hyperinflation (typically defined as monthly inflation exceeding 50%).

questions.topic: Substitution Bias in a Fixed-Basket CPI
questions.title: Substitution Bias in a Fixed-Basket CPI
questions.prompt_template: Which scenario best illustrates why 'substitution bias' causes a fixed-basket Consumer Price Index to overstate true increases in the cost of living?

hints.text: Think about how rational shoppers respond when the price of one grocery item spikes while a close substitute stays cheap.
Remember that a Laspeyres CPI freezes base-year quantities in the market basket.

options_template.text: Beef prices surge by 30%, prompting households to buy more chicken instead, while the CPI continues weighting beef at its higher base-year consumption share.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because fixed base-year weights ignore consumers substituting away from relatively expensive items toward cheaper alternatives, the CPI overstates the true cost of maintaining living standards.

options_template.text: A new smartphone costs $50 more than last year's model but features twice the processing speed and battery life.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Quality Bias vs. Substitution Bias): Improved product performance at a higher price describes quality bias, not consumer substitution across goods.

options_template.text: Streaming video subscriptions become widespread years before BLS statisticians add them to the urban consumer basket.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (New-Product Bias): Delayed inclusion of newly invented goods describes new-product bias rather than relative-price substitution.

options_template.text: Domestic steel mills raise wholesale prices paid by U.S. automobile manufacturers.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Producer vs. Consumer Index): Wholesale input prices paid by firms are tracked by the Producer Price Index (PPI), not the CPI.

questions.topic: Economic Costs of High Inflation: Shoe-Leather, Menu, and Unit-of-Account Costs
questions.title: Economic Costs of High Inflation: Shoe-Leather, Menu, and Unit-of-Account Costs
questions.prompt_template: When high inflation forces restaurants to reprint menus frequently and online retailers to continually update price tags and supplier catalogs, economists classify these wasted real resources as:

hints.text: Distinguish the three textbook resource costs of inflation: shoe-leather costs, menu costs, and unit-of-account distortions.
Focus on the direct administrative and physical cost of changing posted prices.

options_template.text: Menu costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Menu costs are the real labor, printing, and system-update resources firms expend to change nominal prices.

options_template.text: Shoe-leather costs.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Shoe-Leather vs. Menu Costs): Shoe-leather costs refer to the time and transaction effort people spend minimizing cash holdings during high inflation.

options_template.text: Unit-of-account costs.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Unit-of-Account vs. Menu Costs): Unit-of-account costs arise because inflation makes the dollar a less reliable measuring stick for accounting profits and taxes.

options_template.text: Outlet substitution bias.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Measurement Bias vs. Economic Cost): Outlet substitution bias is a statistical bias in how the CPI is calculated when shoppers switch to discount stores.

questions.topic: Producer Price Index (PPI) as an Early Pipeline Indicator
questions.title: Producer Price Index (PPI) as an Early Pipeline Indicator
questions.prompt_template: Why do macroeconomists closely monitor the Producer Price Index (FRED: PPIACO) alongside the Consumer Price Index (FRED: CPIAUCSL)?

hints.text: Consider where raw materials and wholesale goods sit in the supply chain relative to retail store shelves.
Recall what prices the PPI measures.

options_template.text: Because the PPI tracks wholesale prices received by domestic producers, increases in producer input and factory-gate costs often pass through to retail consumer prices later.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Wholesale commodity and producer price changes frequently serve as an early warning signal before retail consumer prices adjust.

options_template.text: Because the PPI measures retail prices of imported luxury goods excluded from the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Import & Retail Coverage): The PPI tracks domestic producer selling prices, whereas imported consumer goods are included in the CPI.

options_template.text: Because Social Security COLAs and federal income tax brackets are legally indexed to the PPI rather than the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Statutory Indexation): Federal benefits and tax brackets are indexed to consumer price indexes (CPI), not the PPI.

options_template.text: Because the PPI is always identical to the GDP Implicit Price Deflator in every quarter.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Index Equivalence): The GDP Deflator covers all final domestic goods and services (C, I, G, X), whereas the PPI covers wholesale producer transactions.

questions.topic: Aggregate Price Level and Base Period Normalization
questions.title: Aggregate Price Level and Base Period Normalization
questions.prompt_template: What does a Consumer Price Index value of 100.0 in the base period indicate?

hints.text: Recall how any market-basket price index is constructed relative to the chosen base period.
Substitute t = 0 into CPI_t = (Cost of Market Basket_t / Cost of Market Basket_0) * 100.

options_template.text: The cost of the fixed market basket in the base period equals itself, normalizing the index to 100.0 as a reference benchmark for comparing other periods.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By construction, dividing the base-period basket cost by itself and multiplying by 100 always yields 100.0, providing a clean reference benchmark.

options_template.text: The typical urban household spent exactly $100.00 on all goods and services during the base year.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Index vs. Dollar Cost): A price index of 100.0 is a normalized ratio, not a literal $100 expenditure; the actual basket cost could be $500 or $50,000.

options_template.text: The economy experienced 100% inflation during the base year.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Price Level vs. Inflation Rate): An index value of 100.0 measures the reference price level, not a 100% annual inflation rate.

options_template.text: Every individual good in the market basket had an identical retail price of $1.00 in the base period.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Individual vs. Aggregate Prices): The aggregate price level summarizes a weighted average of many differently priced goods and services.

questions.topic: Quality and New-Product Bias in the CPI
questions.title: Quality and New-Product Bias in the CPI
questions.prompt_template: How do unmeasured product quality improvements and the delayed introduction of newly invented goods bias the standard Consumer Price Index?

hints.text: Think about what happens when a higher sticker price partly reflects superior performance rather than pure inflation.
Consider also what happens to the prices of newly invented electronics during their early years before they enter the fixed CPI basket.

options_template.text: They bias the CPI upward, causing it to overstate true cost-of-living increases.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Treating quality-driven price increases as pure inflation and missing steep early price drops of new products both cause the fixed-basket CPI to overstate true inflation.

options_template.text: They bias the CPI downward, causing it to systematically understate true inflation.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Bias Direction): Both quality/new-product bias and substitution bias push measured CPI inflation above true cost-of-living growth, not below it.

options_template.text: They cancel each other out exactly so that the fixed-basket CPI has zero measurement error.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Canceling Biases): Both unmeasured quality gains and delayed inclusion of new products bias the CPI in the same upward direction.

options_template.text: They affect only the Producer Price Index (PPI) because consumer electronics are excluded from the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (CPI Coverage): Smartphones, laptops, and other consumer electronics are directly included in the urban household CPI basket.

questions.topic: Outlet Substitution Bias in the CPI
questions.title: Outlet Substitution Bias in the CPI
questions.prompt_template: Which household shopping behavior creates 'outlet substitution bias' in the Consumer Price Index?

hints.text: Focus on the word 'outlet'—where consumers shop rather than which specific food item they buy.
Think about how prices at discount warehouse clubs and online retailers compare to traditional brick-and-mortar retail stores.

options_template.text: Shoppers switch from traditional full-price stores to discount warehouse clubs and online retailers when prices rise, paying less than traditional store surveys record.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Outlet substitution bias arises when consumers move their purchases to lower-priced retail outlets faster than CPI store samples adjust.

options_template.text: Shoppers replace beef with chicken at the same neighborhood supermarket after beef prices spike.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Product vs. Outlet Substitution): Switching from beef to chicken is commodity substitution bias, not outlet substitution bias.

options_template.text: Manufacturers replace domestic steel with imported aluminum to lower factory production costs.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Producer Input Choice): Factory input substitution affects producer costs rather than household retail outlet sampling.

options_template.text: Consumers upgrade to a more expensive laptop that has double the memory and battery life.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Quality Bias vs. Outlet Bias): Paying more for an improved product relates to quality bias, not switching retail outlets.

questions.topic: Laspeyres, Paasche, and Chained CPI Weighting Formulas
questions.title: Laspeyres, Paasche, and Chained CPI Weighting Formulas
questions.prompt_template: How does the Chained Consumer Price Index (FRED: SUUR0000SA0) address the substitution bias built into a standard Laspeyres CPI?

hints.text: Recall that a Laspeyres index holds base-period quantities fixed, whereas a Paasche index uses current-period quantities.
Think about how combining adjacent-period weights captures real-time consumer substitution across categories.

options_template.text: It takes a geometric mean of adjacent-period Laspeyres and Paasche ratios to capture consumer substitution across categories in real time.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The Chained CPI uses a superlative formula combining adjacent-period base and current weights, mitigating the upward substitution bias of a fixed-weight Laspeyres index.

options_template.text: It permanently locks market-basket quantities at their 1982–1984 base-period levels forever.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Fixed Laspeyres Weighting): Locking quantities permanently at base-period levels worsens substitution bias rather than correcting it.

options_template.text: It excludes all housing, food, and energy prices from the market basket to eliminate price volatility.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Chained vs. Core CPI): Chaining refers to updating expenditure weights across periods, not dropping major spending categories.

options_template.text: It replaces retail consumer prices with wholesale commodity prices from the Producer Price Index.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (CPI vs. PPI): The Chained CPI still measures urban retail consumer prices, not wholesale producer selling prices.

questions.topic: Shoe-Leather Costs of High Inflation
questions.title: Shoe-Leather Costs of High Inflation
questions.prompt_template: During episodes of high inflation, why do households and businesses incur 'shoe-leather costs'?

hints.text: Consider what happens to the purchasing power of cash sitting idle in a wallet or zero-interest checking account when prices climb rapidly.
Think about the time and transaction effort required to keep cash balances as small as possible.

options_template.text: Because rapid inflation erodes the purchasing power of cash, people expend extra time and effort making frequent trips to banks or transferring funds to minimize cash holdings.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Shoe-leather costs measure the real time, convenience, and transaction resources wasted trying to hold less currency as inflation taxes cash balances.

options_template.text: Because inflation raises the price of leather footwear faster than the price of groceries and housing.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Literal Interpretation): 'Shoe-leather' is a metaphor for the transaction effort of frequent bank trips, not a statement about footwear prices.

options_template.text: Because restaurants and retailers must spend labor and printing supplies updating posted price lists.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Menu Costs vs. Shoe-Leather Costs): Reprinting menus and changing posted price tags are menu costs, not shoe-leather costs.

options_template.text: Because investors owe capital gains taxes on nominal asset appreciation that reflects zero real gain.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Unit-of-Account vs. Shoe-Leather Costs): Tax distortions on illusory nominal gains are unit-of-account costs.

questions.topic: Unit-of-Account Costs of Inflation
questions.title: Unit-of-Account Costs of Inflation
questions.prompt_template: Which situation best exemplifies a 'unit-of-account cost' of inflation?

hints.text: Recall that money serves as a yardstick for measuring contracts, accounting profits, and taxable gains.
Ask what happens when inflation makes that dollar yardstick shrink over time.

options_template.text: An asset's dollar price rises 10% solely due to 10% inflation, yet tax rules treat the nominal gain as taxable income even though the owner earned zero real gain.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Unit-of-account costs arise because inflation turns the dollar into a shrinking measuring rod, distorting accounting profits, capital gains taxes, and long-term planning.

options_template.text: A grocery store hires extra night-shift workers to replace paper shelf tags every week.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Menu Costs): Spending labor and materials to change posted prices is a menu cost, not a unit-of-account cost.

options_template.text: A commuter visits the ATM three times a week instead of once a month to avoid holding idle cash.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Shoe-Leather Costs): Extra trips to manage cash balances are shoe-leather costs.

options_template.text: A household switches from shopping at a local boutique to buying in bulk at a discount warehouse club.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Outlet Substitution Bias): Switching retail stores is a CPI measurement bias rather than a unit-of-account cost.

questions.topic: Indexation, COLAs, and Preventing Tax Bracket Creep
questions.title: Indexation, COLAs, and Preventing Tax Bracket Creep
questions.prompt_template: What is the primary purpose of indexing federal income tax brackets to the Consumer Price Index?

hints.text: Think about what happens to a worker's nominal income if wages simply keep pace with inflation while tax bracket dollar thresholds stay frozen.
Recall the definition of 'bracket creep' from Section 5.3.

options_template.text: To prevent bracket creep—ensuring households are not pushed into higher marginal tax brackets solely because nominal incomes rose with inflation while real incomes stayed flat.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Indexing tax brackets shifts dollar thresholds upward with the CPI so that inflation alone does not raise a household's effective marginal tax rate.

options_template.text: To guarantee that real interest rates on all bank savings accounts remain strictly positive.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Tax Policy vs. Interest Rates): Tax-bracket indexation adjusts income tax thresholds, not commercial bank deposit rates.

options_template.text: To eliminate substitution bias and quality bias from the BLS calculation of the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Indexation vs. Index Construction): Indexing taxes uses the published CPI; it does not alter how the BLS constructs the index.

options_template.text: To ensure that nominal wages automatically fall during periods of disinflation.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Disinflation and Wages): Disinflation still involves rising prices, and tax-bracket indexation does not reduce nominal wages.

questions.topic: Money Neutrality and Nominal vs. Real Variables
questions.title: Money Neutrality and Nominal vs. Real Variables
questions.prompt_template: Suppose every wage, pension, debt contract, and product price in an economy doubled overnight. According to the principle of long-run money neutrality, what would happen to households' real purchasing power?

hints.text: Divide both the nominal wage and the aggregate price level by 2 (or multiply both by 2) in W_real = (W_nom / CPI) * 100.
Distinguish between dollar labels (nominal variables) and physical goods and services (real variables).

options_template.text: Real purchasing power would remain completely unchanged because every nominal income and every nominal price rose by the exact same proportion.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under money neutrality, doubling all nominal dollar figures leaves relative prices and real purchasing power untouched.

options_template.text: Real purchasing power would double because every worker's paycheck contains twice as many dollars.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Money Illusion): Focusing only on the doubled dollar paycheck ignores that all goods and services also cost twice as much.

options_template.text: Real purchasing power would fall by half because the aggregate price level doubled.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ignoring Nominal Income Adjustment): Real purchasing power falls by half only if nominal incomes stay fixed while prices double; here incomes also doubled.

options_template.text: Real purchasing power would fall to zero because the Consumer Price Index exceeded 100.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Index Threshold Fallacy): An index above 100 simply reflects a higher nominal price level than the base year, not zero purchasing power.

questions.topic: Interpreting Price Index Trajectories Across Inflation and Deflation
questions.title: Interpreting Price Index Trajectories Across Inflation and Deflation
questions.prompt_template: On a time-series graph plotting the Consumer Price Index (vertical axis) against Years (horizontal axis), the plotted line rises steeply from 100.0 in Year 0 to 110.0 in Year 1, and then slopes downward to 107.8 in Year 2. What occurred between Year 1 and Year 2?

hints.text: Look at the slope of the price index line between Year 1 and Year 2.
When the index number itself falls from 110.0 to 107.8, is the inflation rate positive or negative?

options_template.text: Deflation of 2.0%, because the aggregate price index fell outright below its Year 1 level.
options_template.feedback: Correct. A downward-sloping price index indicates a falling aggregate price level: (107.8 - 110.0) / 110.0 = -2.0% deflation.

options_template.text: Disinflation, because the price index remained above its Year 0 base level of 100.0.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Level Above Base vs. Year-over-Year Change): Even though 107.8 is higher than Year 0's 100.0, prices fell relative to Year 1 (110.0), which is deflation.

options_template.text: Inflation of 7.8%, because the Year 2 index stands 7.8 points above 100.0.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Cumulative Change vs. Annual Rate): 7.8% is the cumulative price change since Year 0, not the annual inflation rate between Year 1 and Year 2.

options_template.text: Deflation of 2.2%, found by subtracting 110.0 from 107.8 without dividing by Year 1's index.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Index Point Difference vs. Percentage Rate): -2.2 is the change in index points; dividing by 110.0 gives the percentage rate of -2.0%.

questions.topic: Reading an Inflation-Rate Time-Series Chart During Disinflation
questions.title: Reading an Inflation-Rate Time-Series Chart During Disinflation
questions.prompt_template: On a chart plotting the annual inflation rate pi_t (vertical axis) over time (horizontal axis), the curve remains strictly above the 0% horizontal reference line but slopes downward from +8.0% in 2022 to +3.0% in 2024. How must the corresponding Consumer Price Index (CPI) level be moving between 2022 and 2024?

hints.text: Check the sign of pi_t everywhere between 2022 and 2024: it stays above 0%.
If the percentage growth rate of a variable is positive (+3.0%), does the level of that variable rise or fall?

options_template.text: The CPI level continues rising every year, but at a progressively slower pace (disinflation).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because pi_t > 0 throughout the interval, the price level keeps climbing; the downward slope of pi_t simply indicates slower growth (disinflation).

options_template.text: The CPI level falls steadily back toward its 2022 starting level.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Confusing Rate Slope with Level Slope): For the CPI level to fall, the plotted inflation curve would have to drop below the 0% line into negative territory.

options_template.text: The CPI level remains completely flat and unchanged between 2022 and 2024.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Constant Price Level Condition): A flat price level requires pi_t = 0%, whereas here pi_t remains strictly positive.

options_template.text: The CPI level falls whenever pi_t is below 5.0% and rises only when pi_t exceeds 5.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Arbitrary Threshold): The boundary between rising and falling prices is strictly 0% inflation, not 5.0%.

questions.topic: Visualizing Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Charts
questions.title: Visualizing Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Charts
questions.prompt_template: In a side-by-side comparison chart, a worker's nominal hourly wage bar rises by 4.0% from Period 0 to Period 1, while the real hourly wage bar (measured in constant base-period dollars) shrinks by 0.95%. What must be true about the Consumer Price Index over that period?

hints.text: Compare the growth rate of the nominal wage (+4.0%) with the direction of the real wage (-0.95%).
Real purchasing power falls only when consumer prices grow faster than nominal wages.

options_template.text: The CPI rose by approximately 5.0%, outpacing the 4.0% nominal wage increase.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When inflation (~5.0%) exceeds nominal wage growth (+4.0%), real purchasing power falls by roughly 1.04/1.05 - 1 = -0.95%.

options_template.text: The CPI fell by 4.95%, creating deflation that reduced the real value of paychecks.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Deflation Effect on Real Wages): Falling consumer prices (deflation) would increase the purchasing power of a rising nominal wage, not shrink it.

options_template.text: The CPI rose by exactly 0.95%, matching the decline in the real wage bar.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ignoring Nominal Growth): If the CPI rose by only 0.95% while nominal wages rose 4.0%, real wages would have risen by about 3.0%.

options_template.text: The CPI remained unchanged at 100, but higher income taxes reduced the real wage bar.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Definition of Real Wage): Real wages adjust nominal wages specifically for changes in the aggregate price level (CPI), not tax rates.

questions.topic: Decomposing the Fisher Equation Bar Diagram
questions.title: Decomposing the Fisher Equation Bar Diagram
questions.prompt_template: On a horizontal bar diagram decomposing a 7.0% fixed nominal loan rate (i = 7.0%), the lender and borrower initially anticipate 3.0% inflation (pi^e = 3.0%) and a 4.0% expected real return (r^e = 4.0%). If actual inflation surges to 6.0% (pi = 6.0%), how does the bar partition shift ex post?

hints.text: Keep the total fixed nominal loan rate bar locked at i = 7.0%.
Subtract actual inflation (6.0%) from the fixed nominal rate (7.0%) to find the realized real return.

options_template.text: The inflation segment expands to 6.0% and the lender's realized real return shrinks to 1.0%, transferring 3.0 percentage points of real wealth from the lender to the borrower.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because i is fixed at 7.0%, r_actual = 7.0% - 6.0% = 1.0%, meaning unexpected inflation of 3.0% redistributes purchasing power from creditor to debtor.

options_template.text: The total nominal rate bar automatically expands to 10.0% so the lender keeps a 4.0% real return.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Fixed vs. Variable Contract): On a fixed-rate loan, the nominal rate i is locked in at signing and cannot adjust ex post to inflation surprises.

options_template.text: The lender's realized real return rises to 7.0% while the borrower absorbs a 6.0% real loss.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Redistribution): Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers repay loans in cheaper dollars and hurts lenders.

options_template.text: The realized real interest rate becomes -3.0%, calculated by subtracting actual inflation (6.0%) from expected inflation (3.0%).
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Formula Error): Realized real interest is r_actual = i - pi (7.0% - 6.0% = 1.0%), not pi^e - pi.

questions.topic: Comparing CPI, PPI, and GDP Deflator Attributes (Figure 5.1)
questions.title: Comparing CPI, PPI, and GDP Deflator Attributes
questions.prompt_template: In a three-column comparison chart of U.S. aggregate price indexes (CPI, PPI, and GDP Price Deflator), which index sits in the column characterized by BOTH 'Imports: Excluded' and 'Weights: Current-period changing quantities'?

hints.text: Eliminate the index that includes imported consumer goods first.
Between the two remaining indexes, recall which one is derived directly from Nominal GDP / Real GDP each quarter.

options_template.text: The GDP Implicit Price Deflator.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The GDP Deflator covers all current domestically produced final goods and services (C, I, G, X), excludes imports, and automatically updates its expenditure weights each period.

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI).
options_template.feedback: Misconception (CPI Attributes): The standard CPI includes imported consumer goods and uses fixed short-run base-period basket weights.

options_template.text: The Producer Price Index (PPI).
options_template.feedback: Misconception (PPI Attributes): Although the PPI excludes imports, it tracks wholesale domestic producer prices rather than current-period final GDP weights across C, I, G, and X.

options_template.text: None of the three indexes excludes imported goods.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Import Rules): Both the PPI and the GDP Deflator exclude imports because they measure domestic production.

questions.topic: Identifying Disinflation on a Price-Index Level Graph
questions.title: Identifying Disinflation on a Price-Index Level Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a graph plotting the Consumer Price Index (vertical axis) against Years (horizontal axis), the plotted line rises steeply from 100.0 in Year 0 to 110.0 in Year 1 (+10.0%), and then continues sloping upward—but more gently—to 115.5 in Year 2. How is the Year 1 to Year 2 segment classified?

hints.text: Check whether the CPI line is still sloping upward (prices rising) or sloping downward (prices falling).
Compare the Year 2 percentage growth rate ((115.5 - 110.0)/110.0 = +5.0%) to Year 1's +10.0%.

options_template.text: Disinflation, because the price index is still rising (+5.0%), just at a slower annual rate than in Year 1 (+10.0%).
options_template.feedback: Correct. An upward-sloping CPI line with a flatter slope reflects positive but slower inflation—the exact graphical signature of disinflation.

options_template.text: Deflation, because the line became flatter in Year 2 than in Year 1.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Flatter Positive Slope vs. Negative Slope): Deflation requires the CPI level line to slope downward (negative inflation), not merely flatten while still rising.

options_template.text: Accelerating inflation, because the Year 2 index value (115.5) is higher than Year 1's value (110.0).
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Higher Level vs. Faster Rate): A higher index level means prices rose, but the rate of increase slowed from +10.0% to +5.0%.

options_template.text: Price stability (0% inflation), because the price level rose by less than 10 points.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Zero Inflation Condition): Zero inflation would appear as a completely horizontal (flat) line at 110.0.

questions.topic: Crossing the Zero Line on an Inflation-Rate Chart
questions.title: Crossing the Zero Line on an Inflation-Rate Chart
questions.prompt_template: On a time-series diagram plotting the annual inflation rate pi_t on the vertical axis against Time on the horizontal axis, what exact graphical event signals that an economy has transitioned from disinflation into outright deflation?

hints.text: Recall the sign of pi_t during disinflation versus deflation.
Look at the horizontal reference line at pi_t = 0%.

options_template.text: The plotted inflation-rate curve crosses below the horizontal 0% line into negative territory (pi_t < 0).
options_template.feedback: Correct. As long as the downward-sloping curve stays above 0%, the economy is in disinflation; crossing below 0% means the aggregate price level begins falling outright (deflation).

options_template.text: The plotted inflation-rate curve reaches its peak and begins sloping downward while still above 0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Peak vs. Zero Crossing): Turning downward above 0% marks the onset of disinflation, not deflation.

options_template.text: The plotted inflation-rate curve crosses below the central bank's 2.0% inflation target.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Target vs. Zero Boundary): Inflation of +1.5% is below a 2.0% target, yet prices are still rising rather than deflating.

options_template.text: The plotted inflation-rate curve flattens out horizontally at +3.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Constant Positive Inflation): A flat line at +3.0% means steady 3.0% inflation, not deflation.

questions.topic: Comparing Accelerating Inflation and Disinflation Segments on a Rate Chart
questions.title: Comparing Accelerating Inflation and Disinflation Segments on a Rate Chart
questions.prompt_template: On an inflation-rate chart (pi_t vs. Time), Segment A slopes upward from +2.0% to +6.0%, and Segment B slopes downward from +6.0% to +2.0%. Which statement accurately compares the aggregate price level across both segments?

hints.text: Check whether pi_t is positive or negative during Segment A and during Segment B.
Remember that any positive inflation rate means the aggregate price level is increasing.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level rises throughout both Segment A and Segment B, accelerating during Segment A and slowing (disinflating) during Segment B.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because pi_t > 0 in both segments, the price level climbs continuously—faster during Segment A and more slowly during Segment B.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level rises during Segment A and falls back to its starting level during Segment B.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Symmetry Fallacy): Because Segment B remains above 0%, prices keep rising rather than returning to their earlier level.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level is lower at the end of Segment B than at the peak between Segments A and B.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Rate Peak vs. Price-Level Peak): The price level continues rising after the inflation rate peaks as long as pi_t stays positive.

options_template.text: The aggregate price level is constant during Segment B because the inflation rate is falling.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Falling Rate vs. Zero Rate): A falling positive rate still adds positive price increases each period.

questions.topic: Reading a Dual-Series PPI vs. CPI Pipeline Chart
questions.title: Reading a Dual-Series PPI vs. CPI Pipeline Chart
questions.prompt_template: On a FRED time-series graph plotting annual percentage changes in PPIACO (Producer Price Index) and CPIAUCSL (Consumer Price Index) during a supply-chain disruption, the PPIACO curve spikes sharply and peaks several months before the CPIAUCSL curve peaks. What economic mechanism explains this visual lead-lag pattern?

hints.text: Think about where wholesale commodities and factory inputs sit in the production chain relative to retail checkout prices.
Recall the pipeline role of the PPI from Section 5.1.

options_template.text: Wholesale commodity, freight, and producer input price increases occur earlier in the supply chain and gradually pass through into retail consumer prices.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because PPI tracks wholesale prices received by domestic producers, surges in input and factory-gate costs typically show up in PPIACO before reaching retail shelves in CPIAUCSL.

options_template.text: The BLS publishes the CPI six months later than the PPI by law, creating an artificial calendar delay.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Publication Lag): Both CPIAUCSL and PPIACO are published monthly on similar schedules; the lead-lag reflects supply-chain pass-through.

options_template.text: Consumers stop buying retail goods whenever the PPI rises, forcing retail prices to jump later.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Demand Response): Lower consumer demand would put downward—not upward—pressure on retail prices.

options_template.text: The PPI includes imported consumer electronics while the CPI excludes them.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Import Coverage): Imported consumer goods are included in the CPI and excluded from the PPI.

questions.topic: Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Chart Under Deflation
questions.title: Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Chart Under Deflation
questions.prompt_template: In a side-by-side bar chart comparing Period 0 and Period 1, a worker's nominal hourly wage bar stays completely unchanged at $20.00 in both periods, yet the worker's real hourly wage bar (in constant base-period dollars) becomes visibly taller in Period 1. What must have happened to the Consumer Price Index between Period 0 and Period 1?

hints.text: Use W_real = (W_nom / CPI) * 100 with W_nom held constant.
Ask how the denominator (CPI) must move for W_real to increase when the numerator (W_nom) is fixed.

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index fell (deflation), increasing the real purchasing power of the unchanged $20.00 nominal wage.
options_template.feedback: Correct. With W_nom fixed at $20.00, W_real = ($20.00 / CPI) * 100 rises only if CPI decreases (pi < 0, deflation).

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index rose (inflation), lifting the real wage bar above the nominal wage bar.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inflation Direction): A higher CPI increases the denominator and shrinks the real wage bar.

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index experienced disinflation, meaning prices rose more slowly than before.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Disinflation vs. Deflation): During disinflation, the CPI is still rising, which would shrink—not raise—the real value of a fixed $20.00 nominal wage.

options_template.text: The Consumer Price Index stayed constant while the base year was renamed.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Unchanged Price Level): If both nominal wages and the price level are unchanged, real purchasing power cannot rise.

questions.topic: Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Chart with Exact Inflation Matching
questions.title: Nominal vs. Real Wage Bar Chart with Exact Inflation Matching
questions.prompt_template: In a side-by-side wage comparison chart, the nominal wage bar grows by 5.0% from Period 0 to Period 1, while the real wage bar remains the exact same height in both periods. What does this visual pattern imply about CPI inflation over the period?

hints.text: Recall the relationship 1 + g_real = (1 + g_W) / (1 + pi).
If g_real = 0% and g_W = +5.0%, what must pi equal?

options_template.text: CPI inflation was exactly 5.0%, fully offsetting the 5.0% nominal raise and leaving real purchasing power unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When nominal wage growth (+5.0%) equals CPI inflation (+5.0%), (1.05 / 1.05) - 1 = 0%, so the real wage bar stays flat.

options_template.text: CPI inflation was 0%, which is why the real wage bar did not move.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Confusing Real Change with Inflation): If CPI inflation were 0% while nominal wages rose 5.0%, the real wage bar would also grow by 5.0%.

options_template.text: CPI inflation was 10.0%, twice as large as the nominal wage increase.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Over-Erosion): If inflation were 10.0% against a 5.0% raise, the real wage bar would visibly shrink.

options_template.text: The economy experienced 5.0% deflation, canceling out the 5.0% nominal raise.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Sign of Deflation): Deflation of 5.0% combined with a 5.0% nominal raise would boost the real wage bar by over 10%.

questions.topic: Fisher Equation Bar Diagram Under Unexpected Disinflation
questions.title: Fisher Equation Bar Diagram Under Unexpected Disinflation
questions.prompt_template: On a horizontal bar diagram decomposing a fixed nominal loan rate of i = 7.0%, the ex-ante bar is split into a 4.0% expected real return (r^e) and 3.0% expected inflation (pi^e). If actual inflation drops unexpectedly to pi = 1.0%, how does the ex-post bar partition change?

hints.text: Keep the total bar width fixed at i = 7.0%.
Shrink the actual inflation segment to 1.0% and measure the remaining width for the realized real return.

options_template.text: The inflation segment shrinks to 1.0% and the lender's realized real return expands to 6.0%, transferring 2.0 percentage points of real wealth from the borrower to the lender.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because i stays fixed at 7.0%, r_actual = 7.0% - 1.0% = 6.0%, which is 2.0 percentage points higher than r^e = 4.0%—benefiting the lender at the borrower's expense.

options_template.text: The inflation segment shrinks to 1.0% and the total nominal rate bar shrinks to 5.0% so the borrower's real cost stays at 4.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Fixed-Rate Rigidity): On a fixed-rate loan, the nominal interest rate is locked at 7.0% and does not fall ex post when inflation slows.

options_template.text: The lender's realized real return falls to 2.0%, transferring 2.0 percentage points of real wealth from the lender to the borrower.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Redistribution): Unexpectedly low inflation increases the real value of repaid dollars, helping lenders and hurting borrowers.

options_template.text: The realized real return rises to 8.0% because lower inflation adds 1.0% onto the 7.0% nominal rate.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Sign Error): Positive 1.0% inflation still erodes 1.0% of the 7.0% nominal return (r_actual = 7.0% - 1.0% = 6.0%); only outright deflation (pi < 0) makes r exceed i.

questions.topic: Fisher Equation Bar Diagram Showing a Negative Real Interest Rate
questions.title: Fisher Equation Bar Diagram Showing a Negative Real Interest Rate
questions.prompt_template: On a horizontal bar diagram of a fixed-rate loan with nominal interest rate i = 5.0%, the actual inflation erosion bar extends all the way to pi = 8.0%—exceeding the 5.0% nominal rate bar by 3.0 percentage points. What does this diagram visually depict?

hints.text: Compute r_actual = i - pi when i = 5.0% and pi = 8.0%.
Determine whether the lender gained or lost real purchasing power over the life of the loan.

options_template.text: A negative realized real interest rate of r_actual = -3.0%, meaning the lender loses 3.0% in real purchasing power despite receiving 5.0% more dollars.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Whenever actual inflation (8.0%) exceeds the nominal interest rate (5.0%), the realized real rate turns negative (5.0% - 8.0% = -3.0%), eroding the lender's real wealth.

options_template.text: A realized real interest rate of +3.0%, because we always subtract the smaller number from the larger number.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Absolute Value Error): The Fisher Equation is strictly r = i - pi; reversing the order hides the negative real return.

options_template.text: A realized real interest rate of 0.0%, because real interest rates are legally floored at zero.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Zero Lower Bound Confusion): Real interest rates have no zero lower bound and frequently turn negative when inflation exceeds nominal rates.

options_template.text: A nominal interest rate of -3.0%, meaning the bank pays the borrower cash to take out the loan.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Nominal vs. Real Rate): The nominal rate remains +5.0%; it is the real purchasing-power return that is -3.0%.

questions.topic: Constructing a Market-Basket CPI
questions.title: Constructing a Market-Basket CPI
questions.prompt_template: A representative urban market basket contains 10 units of housing and 50 units of food. In the base year (Year 0), housing costs $30 per unit and food costs $4 per unit. In Year 1, housing rises to $33 per unit and food rises to $4.40 per unit. What is the CPI in Year 1?

hints.text: Step 1: Multiply base-year prices by the fixed basket quantities to find Cost of Market Basket_0.
Step 2: Multiply Year 1 prices by the exact same fixed basket quantities to find Cost of Market Basket_1, then compute (Basket_1 / Basket_0) * 100.

options_template.text: 110.0 (for Base Basket = $500 and Year 1 Basket = $550)
90.9 (dividing Base Basket $500 by Year 1 Basket $550)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inverted Ratio): Dividing Basket_0 by Basket_1 inverts the price index formula.

options_template.text: 150.0 (adding the $50 dollar increase directly to 100)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Dollar Change vs. Percentage Index): Adding raw dollar changes ($50) to 100 ignores the base-year denominator ($500).

options_template.text: 110.0% (reporting an index level as a percentage growth rate)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Units Error): A price index is a pure unitless index number (110.0), whereas the inflation rate is a percentage (+10.0%).

questions.topic: Computing the GDP Implicit Price Deflator
questions.title: Computing the GDP Implicit Price Deflator
questions.prompt_template: In a given year, an economy produces Nominal GDP of $27,500 billion and Real GDP of $25,000 billion. What is the economy's GDP Implicit Price Deflator?

hints.text: Use the identity: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) * 100.
Verify that when Nominal GDP exceeds Real GDP, the GDP Deflator must be greater than 100.

options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inverted Formula): Dividing Real GDP by Nominal GDP ($25,000 / $27,500 * 100) inverts the GDP Deflator formula.
Misconception (Omitting Base 100): 10.0% is the cumulative price change above the base year, not the index level itself (100 + 10.0 = 110.0).
Misconception (Dollar Gap): $2,500 billion is the nominal-minus-real dollar difference, not the price index.

questions.topic: Calculating Annual Inflation and Deflation Rates Across Multiple Years
questions.title: Calculating Annual Inflation and Deflation Rates Across Multiple Years
questions.prompt_template: An economy's Consumer Price Index is 100.0 in Year 0, 110.0 in Year 1, and 107.8 in Year 2. What is the annual inflation rate in Year 2?

hints.text: Always use the immediately preceding year's index (CPI_1 = 110.0) in the denominator, not the Year 0 base index.

options_template.text: -2.0% (deflation)
-2.2% (deflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Wrong Denominator): Subtracting 110.0 from 107.8 gives -2.2 index points; dividing by Year 0's base 100 instead of Year 1's 110.0 yields -2.2%.

options_template.text: +7.8% (inflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Comparing to Base Year Instead of Prior Year): +7.8% measures cumulative price growth since Year 0, not the annual rate in Year 2.

options_template.text: +2.0% (disinflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Sign Error): Because CPI_2 (107.8) is lower than CPI_1 (110.0), the percentage change is negative (-2.0%), not positive.

questions.topic: Converting Nominal Wages into Constant-Dollar Real Wages
questions.title: Converting Nominal Wages into Constant-Dollar Real Wages
questions.prompt_template: A worker's nominal hourly wage rises from $20.00 in Period 0 to $20.80 in Period 1 (+4.0%), while the Consumer Price Index rises from 300 in Period 0 to 315 in Period 1 (+5.0%). What is the worker's real hourly wage in Period 1 (expressed in base-period dollars where CPI = 100), and by what percentage did real purchasing power change?

hints.text: Compare W_real_1 to W_real_0 using (W_real_1 / W_real_0) - 1, or use the exact Fisher ratio (1.04 / 1.05) - 1.

options_template.text: $6.603 per hour; real purchasing power fell by approximately 0.95%.
options_template.feedback: Correct. W_real_1 = ($20.80 / 315) * 100 = $6.603, down from W_real_0 = $6.667—a percentage change of (6.603 / 6.667) - 1 = -0.95%.

options_template.text: $6.933 per hour; real purchasing power rose by 4.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Deflating by Old CPI): Dividing the new wage ($20.80) by the old CPI (300) ignores the 5.0% increase in consumer prices.

options_template.text: $6.603 per hour; real purchasing power rose by 9.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Adding Wage Growth and Inflation): Inflation erodes nominal raises rather than adding to them; subtract or divide by (1 + pi) rather than adding.

options_template.text: $65.52 per hour; real purchasing power rose by 5.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Multiplying Instead of Dividing by CPI): Multiplying $20.80 by (315 / 100) inflates the wage twice instead of deflating it.

questions.topic: Expected vs. Realized Real Interest Rates (Fisher Equation)
questions.title: Expected vs. Realized Real Interest Rates (Fisher Equation)
questions.prompt_template: A credit union issues a one-year fixed-rate business loan at a nominal interest rate of i = 7.0% when both parties expect inflation to be pi^e = 3.0%. If actual inflation turns out to be pi = 6.0%, what are the expected real interest rate (r^e) and the realized real interest rate (r_actual) using the linear Fisher Equation?

hints.text: Use r^e = i - pi^e for the expected real interest rate at loan signing.
Use r_actual = i - pi for the realized real interest rate after actual inflation is observed.

options_template.text: r^e = 4.0% and r_actual = 1.0%
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expected real rate r^e = 7.0% - 3.0% = 4.0%, while realized real rate r_actual = 7.0% - 6.0% = 1.0%.

options_template.text: r^e = 10.0% and r_actual = 13.0%
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Adding Inflation Instead of Subtracting): Because inflation erodes the purchasing power of repaid dollars, subtract pi from i rather than adding.

options_template.text: r^e = 4.0% and r_actual = 4.0%
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ignoring Inflation Surprise): On a fixed-rate loan, unexpected inflation lowers the realized real return below the expected return.

options_template.text: r^e = 1.0% and r_actual = 4.0%
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Swapping Expected and Actual Inflation): Expected inflation was 3.0% (giving r^e = 4.0%), whereas actual inflation was 6.0% (giving r_actual = 1.0%).

questions.topic: Exact Multiplicative Fisher Compounding
questions.title: Exact Multiplicative Fisher Compounding
questions.prompt_template: Using the exact multiplicative Fisher relation 1 + g_real = (1 + g_W) / (1 + pi), what is the exact real wage growth rate when a worker receives a 3.0% nominal raise (g_W = 0.03) during a year with 6.0% CPI inflation (pi = 0.06)?

hints.text: Substitute g_W = 0.03 and pi = 0.06 into g_real = (1 + g_W) / (1 + pi) - 1.
Compute 1.03 / 1.06 - 1 and convert to a percentage.

options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inverted Ratio): Computing (1.06 / 1.03) - 1 reverses the numerator and denominator.
Misconception (Linear Approximation Instead of Exact Formula): 3.0% - 6.0% = -3.00% is the linear approximation, not the exact compounded result requested.
Misconception (Multiplying Gross Factors): Computing (1.03 * 1.06) - 1 compounds inflation onto the raise instead of deflating by (1 + pi).

questions.topic: Multi-Year Market-Basket CPI and Disinflation Rate
questions.title: Multi-Year Market-Basket CPI and Disinflation Rate
questions.prompt_template: An urban market basket consists of 10 units of housing and 50 units of food. In the base year (Year 0), housing costs $60.00 per unit and food costs $8.00 per unit. In Year 1, prices rise to $66.00 for housing and $8.80 for food. In Year 2, prices rise to $69.30 for housing and $9.24 for food. What is the annual inflation rate in Year 2, and which regime does it represent?

hints.text: First compute Basket_0 = $1,000, Basket_1 = $1,100 (CPI_1 = 110.0), and Basket_2 = $1,155 (CPI_2 = 115.5).
Then compute pi_2 = ((CPI_2 - CPI_1) / CPI_1) * 100% and compare it to Year 1's +10.0% rate.

options_template.text: +5.0% (disinflation)
options_template.feedback: Correct. CPI_1 = 110.0 (+10.0% inflation) and CPI_2 = 115.5, so pi_2 = ((115.5 - 110.0) / 110.0) * 100% = (5.5 / 110.0) * 100% = +5.0%, which is disinflation because inflation slowed from 10.0% to 5.0%.

options_template.text: +5.5% (disinflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Wrong Denominator): Subtracting 110.0 from 115.5 gives 5.5 index points; dividing by Year 0's base 100 instead of Year 1's 110.0 falsely yields +5.5%.

options_template.text: +15.5% (inflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Cumulative vs. Annual Rate): +15.5% is the two-year cumulative price increase since Year 0, not the annual inflation rate in Year 2.

options_template.text: -5.0% (deflation)
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Confusing Disinflation with Deflation): The inflation rate dropped by 5.0 percentage points (from 10.0% to 5.0%), but prices still rose by +5.0% rather than falling.

questions.topic: Solving for Real GDP Using the GDP Implicit Price Deflator
questions.title: Solving for Real GDP Using the GDP Implicit Price Deflator
questions.prompt_template: Suppose an economy reports Nominal GDP of $26,400 billion and a GDP Implicit Price Deflator of 120.0. What is the economy's Real GDP?

hints.text: Start from GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) * 100 and solve algebraically for Real GDP.
Compute Real GDP = (Nominal GDP / GDP Deflator) * 100 = ($26,400 billion / 120.0) * 100.

options_template.text: $22,000 billion
options_template.feedback: Correct. Real GDP = ($26,400 billion / 120.0) * 100 = $220 billion * 100 = $22,000 billion.

options_template.text: $31,680 billion
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Multiplying Instead of Dividing): Multiplying Nominal GDP by 1.20 inflates the figure instead of deflating it to base-year prices.

options_template.text: $220 billion
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Omitting the Factor of 100): Dividing $26,400 billion by 120 without multiplying by 100 understates Real GDP by a factor of 100.

options_template.text: $26,280 billion
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Subtracting the Index): Subtracting the price index (120) directly from Nominal GDP ($26,400 billion) confuses index-ratio deflation with subtraction.

questions.topic: Converting a Historical Salary into Current-Year Dollars
questions.title: Converting a Historical Salary into Current-Year Dollars
questions.prompt_template: In 1990, a newly hired analyst earned a nominal starting salary of $32,000 when the Consumer Price Index was 125.0. If the CPI in 2025 is 312.5, what nominal salary in 2025 provides the exact same real purchasing power as the 1990 salary?

hints.text: Use the cross-period conversion formula: Value in Period B Dollars = Nominal Value_A * (CPI_B / CPI_A).
Compute $32,000 * (312.5 / 125.0) by first simplifying the ratio 312.5 / 125.0 = 2.5.

options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inverted CPI Ratio): Multiplying $32,000 by (125.0 / 312.5) converts 2025 dollars backward into 1990 dollars instead of forward.
Misconception (Using Index Difference Instead of Ratio): Multiplying $32,000 by (312.5 - 125.0) / 100 = 1.875 omits the original base and miscalculates the price-level ratio.
Misconception (Ignoring 1990 CPI): Multiplying $32,000 by (312.5 / 100) treats 1990 as if its CPI were 100.0 instead of 125.0.

questions.topic: Real Hourly Wage Levels and Exact Real Wage Growth
questions.title: Real Hourly Wage Levels and Exact Real Wage Growth
questions.prompt_template: A technician's nominal hourly wage rises from $24.00 in Year 1 (when CPI = 120.0) to $30.00 in Year 2 (when CPI = 125.0). What is the technician's real hourly wage in Year 2 (in base-year dollars), and by what exact percentage did real purchasing power grow?

hints.text: Compute Year 1 real wage: ($24.00 / 120.0) * 100 = $20.00, and Year 2 real wage: ($30.00 / 125.0) * 100.
Then calculate the percentage change from Year 1's real wage to Year 2's real wage.

options_template.text: $24.00 per hour; real purchasing power grew by exactly 20.0%.
$25.00 per hour; real purchasing power grew by 25.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Deflating by Old CPI): Dividing $30.00 by Year 1's CPI (120.0) instead of Year 2's CPI (125.0) ignores the rise in consumer prices.

options_template.text: $24.00 per hour; real purchasing power grew by 25.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reporting Nominal Growth): +25.0% is the nominal wage growth (($30 - $24)/$24), not the inflation-adjusted real wage growth (+20.0%).

options_template.text: $24.00 per hour; real purchasing power grew by 15.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Subtracting Index Points): Subtracting 5 CPI index points from 20% confuses index-point differences with percentage inflation.

questions.topic: Real Interest Rate and Dollar Wealth Redistribution Under Unexpected Disinflation
questions.title: Real Interest Rate and Dollar Wealth Redistribution Under Unexpected Disinflation
questions.prompt_template: A regional bank issues a one-year fixed-rate loan of $20,000 at a nominal interest rate of i = 6.5% when expected inflation is pi^e = 2.5%. Actual inflation turns out to be pi = 1.0%. Using the linear Fisher Equation, what is the realized real interest rate (r_actual), and how much real purchasing power is unexpectedly redistributed?

hints.text: Compute r^e = i - pi^e = 6.5% - 2.5% = 4.0% and r_actual = i - pi = 6.5% - 1.0%.
Multiply the unexpected real-rate gap (r_actual - r^e) by the $20,000 loan principal, and check who wins when actual inflation is lower than expected.

options_template.text: r_actual = 5.5%; $300 in real purchasing power is transferred from the borrower to the lender.
options_template.feedback: Correct. r^e = 4.0% and r_actual = 6.5% - 1.0% = 5.5%. Because actual inflation was 1.5 percentage points lower than expected, 1.5% * $20,000 = $300 in real wealth transfers from borrower to lender.

options_template.text: r_actual = 5.5%; $300 in real purchasing power is transferred from the lender to the borrower.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Redistribution): When actual inflation is lower than expected, repaid dollars buy more goods than anticipated, so the lender wins and the borrower loses.

options_template.text: r_actual = 4.0%; $0 in real purchasing power is redistributed.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ignoring Inflation Surprise): 4.0% was the expected real rate; because pi = 1.0% differed from pi^e = 2.5%, the realized real rate rose to 5.5%.

options_template.text: r_actual = 7.5%; $700 in real purchasing power is transferred from the borrower to the lender.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Adding Inflation to Nominal Rate): Positive 1.0% inflation still subtracts from the nominal rate (6.5% - 1.0% = 5.5%), rather than adding to it.

questions.topic: Exact Multiplicative Fisher Equation Under High Inflation
questions.title: Exact Multiplicative Fisher Equation Under High Inflation
questions.prompt_template: In a high-inflation economy, a one-year bond pays a nominal interest rate of i = 35.0% while actual inflation is pi = 25.0%. Using the exact multiplicative Fisher formula r = (i - pi) / (1 + pi), what is the exact realized real interest rate?

hints.text: Convert percentages to decimals: i = 0.35 and pi = 0.25.

options_template.feedback: Correct. r = (0.35 - 0.25) / (1 + 0.25) = 0.10 / 1.25 = 0.08, or exactly 8.0%—showing why the linear approximation (10.0%) becomes inaccurate at high inflation.
Misconception (Linear Approximation Error): 35.0% - 25.0% = 10.0% ignores the denominator (1 + pi) = 1.25 required by the exact multiplicative Fisher formula.
Misconception (Multiplying by 1 + pi): Multiplying (0.35 - 0.25) by 1.25 instead of dividing yields 12.5%.
Misconception (Adding Nominal Rate and Inflation): Summing 35.0% + 25.0% adds inflation erosion onto the nominal return instead of deflating by it.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Import Price Shocks: CPI vs. GDP Deflator Divergence
questions.title: Import Price Shocks: CPI vs. GDP Deflator Divergence
questions.prompt_template: Suppose global shipping disruptions cause the retail prices of imported European olive oil and imported Japanese automobiles sold in the United States to jump by 20%, while the prices of all domestically produced U.S. goods and services remain completely unchanged. How will the U.S. CPI (CPIAUCSL) and the U.S. GDP Implicit Price Deflator respond?

hints.text: Ask whether imported consumer goods are part of the urban household market basket.
Recall that GDP measures domestic production (Y = C + I + G + X - M), so imports cancel out of domestic GDP.

options_template.text: The U.S. CPI rises because imported consumer goods sit inside the urban consumer basket, whereas the U.S. GDP Deflator stays unchanged because imports are excluded from domestic GDP.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Imported consumer goods affect urban household living costs (CPI) directly, but because GDP tracks only domestic production, import prices do not enter the GDP Deflator.

options_template.text: The U.S. GDP Deflator rises while the U.S. CPI stays unchanged, because international trade is recorded inside GDP.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Net Exports Sign): Imports are subtracted in GDP (NX = X - M) precisely to remove foreign-produced goods from domestic GDP and its deflator.

options_template.text: Both the U.S. CPI and the U.S. GDP Deflator rise by the exact same percentage.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Identical Coverage): The two indexes diverge sharply during foreign import price shocks due to their different import rules.

options_template.text: The U.S. GDP Deflator falls because higher import prices increase M and reduce Nominal GDP.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Accounting Identity Confusion): Higher spending on imports increases C and M equally in Nominal GDP, leaving domestic Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the GDP Deflator unchanged.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Fiscal Budget Impact of CPI Upward Bias on Social Security COLAs
questions.title: Fiscal Budget Impact of CPI Upward Bias on Social Security COLAs
questions.prompt_template: Because the standard Consumer Price Index overstates true cost-of-living increases by roughly 0.5 to 1.0 percentage points per year due to substitution and quality biases, indexing Social Security benefits to the standard CPI rather than the Chained CPI (SUUR0000SA0) causes:

hints.text: Think about what happens to annual Cost-of-Living Adjustments (COLAs) when the reference index grows 0.5–1.0 percentage points faster than true living costs.
Trace the effect on federal outlays and recipients' real purchasing power.

options_template.text: Federal benefit outlays to grow faster than true living costs, slightly increasing recipients' real purchasing power over time while raising long-run federal spending.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because standard CPI overstates true cost-of-living inflation, full CPI indexation gives COLAs slightly larger than needed to hold utility constant, increasing federal outlays.

options_template.text: Retirees' real purchasing power to fall steadily every year because the CPI understates inflation.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Direction of CPI Bias): Fixed-basket biases cause the standard CPI to overstate—not understate—true cost-of-living growth.

options_template.text: Zero effect on the federal budget because Social Security benefits are paid in real goods rather than nominal dollars.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Nominal Benefit Contracts): Social Security pays nominal dollar checks adjusted annually by the statutory COLA formula.

options_template.text: Automatic tax bracket creep that pushes low-income retirees into higher marginal income tax brackets.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Bracket Creep Mechanism): Bracket creep occurs when tax brackets are unindexed; indexing brackets to the standard CPI actually shifts thresholds upward slightly faster than true inflation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Why Central Banks Fear Economy-Wide Deflation (Debt-Deflation Spiral)
questions.title: Why Central Banks Fear Economy-Wide Deflation (Debt-Deflation Spiral)
questions.prompt_template: Why do central banks like the Federal Reserve target a low, positive inflation rate (around 2.0%) rather than 0% or mild deflation?

hints.text: Consider what happens to fixed nominal debt burdens and consumer spending incentives when people expect prices to be lower next year.
Recall the concept of debt deflation and downward nominal wage rigidity.

options_template.text: Deflation raises the real burden of fixed nominal debts, encourages households to delay purchases in anticipation of lower future prices, and risks a self-reinforcing contractionary spiral.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because debts and wages are written in nominal dollars, falling prices raise real debt burdens (debt deflation) and incentivize delayed spending, deepening recessions.

options_template.text: Deflation causes hyperinflation within six months by eliminating all shoe-leather and menu costs.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Opposite Dynamics): Deflation is a falling price level (pi < 0), the opposite of hyperinflation.

options_template.text: A 2.0% inflation target guarantees that nominal wages and real wages always grow at the exact same rate.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Nominal vs. Real Wedge): Under 2.0% inflation, nominal wage growth exceeds real wage growth by roughly 2.0 percentage points.

options_template.text: Deflation transfers real wealth from banks to mortgage borrowers, causing commercial banks to become insolvent.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Redistribution): Deflation transfers real wealth from borrowers to lenders, which can trigger borrower defaults when debtors cannot repay heavier real debts.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Fixed-Rate Mortgages vs. TIPS During an Unexpected Inflation Surge
questions.title: Fixed-Rate Mortgages vs. TIPS During an Unexpected Inflation Surge
questions.prompt_template: In 2020, a homeowner locks in a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at a nominal interest rate of i = 3.2%, while an investor buys Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) paying a guaranteed real yield of r = 0.5%. When U.S. CPI inflation unexpectedly surges above 6.0% in 2022, who benefits from the inflation surprise?

hints.text: Compute the homeowner's realized real mortgage rate (r_actual = i - pi) when pi = 6.0%.
Recall how TIPS principal adjusts to changes in the CPI.

options_template.text: The homeowner benefits from a negative realized real mortgage rate (3.2% - 6.0% = -2.8%), while the TIPS investor's principal adjusts upward with the CPI to preserve the 0.5% real return.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Fixed-rate borrowers win during unexpected inflation because their real borrowing cost turns negative (-2.8%), whereas TIPS index principal to the CPI to protect savers.

options_template.text: The mortgage lender benefits because the homeowner's monthly nominal mortgage payment automatically doubles with the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Fixed-Rate Contract): Fixed-rate mortgage payments remain constant in nominal dollars, eroding the real value received by the lender.

options_template.text: The TIPS investor suffers a realized real return of -5.5% because Treasury bonds are never indexed to inflation.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (TIPS Design): Unlike conventional nominal Treasury notes, TIPS explicitly adjust principal using the CPI (CPIAUCSL).

options_template.text: Neither party is affected because the Fisher Effect forces all existing fixed-rate contracts to reset immediately.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ex-Ante vs. Ex-Post Fisher Effect): The Fisher Effect governs new loan rates priced for expected inflation; existing fixed-rate contracts do not reset.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Diagnosing Negative Real Interest Rates on Savings Accounts
questions.title: Diagnosing Negative Real Interest Rates on Savings Accounts
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a commercial bank offers a savings account paying a nominal interest rate of i = 1.5% per year during a year when CPI inflation (CPIAUCSL) is pi = 4.5%. Which statement accurately evaluates the saver's financial outcome?

hints.text: Calculate the realized real interest rate r = i - pi.
Distinguish between having more dollars in the bank account and being able to buy more goods and services.

options_template.text: The saver ends the year with 1.5% more dollars, but those dollars buy roughly 3.0% fewer goods and services because the realized real interest rate is negative (r = -3.0%).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Nominal balance grows by +1.5%, but 4.5% inflation erodes purchasing power faster, yielding a negative real return of approximately 1.5% - 4.5% = -3.0%.

options_template.text: This outcome is mathematically impossible because real interest rates can never fall below 0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Zero Lower Bound Confusion): Nominal rates rarely fall below zero, but real interest rates (r = i - pi) frequently turn negative whenever inflation exceeds nominal interest.

options_template.text: The saver gains 6.0% in real purchasing power because interest earned and inflation both increase the dollar value of wealth.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Sign of Inflation): Rising prices reduce—not increase—the real purchasing power of a dollar balance.

options_template.text: The saver would have preserved more purchasing power by holding physical cash under a mattress (i = 0%).
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Opportunity Cost of Cash): Holding 0% physical cash yields r = 0% - 4.5% = -4.5%, which loses even more purchasing power than earning 1.5% nominal interest.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Interpreting the 2022–2024 U.S. Disinflation Plateau
questions.title: Interpreting the 2022–2024 U.S. Disinflation Plateau
questions.prompt_template: After U.S. annual CPI inflation (CPIAUCSL) cooled from above 8% in mid-2022 to roughly 3% in 2024, many households remained frustrated that grocery and rent bills were still far above 2019 levels. Which macroeconomic distinction explains why disinflation did not return prices to 2019 levels?

hints.text: Distinguish between a slowdown in the rate of price growth (disinflation) and a fall in the price level itself (deflation).
Ask what +3% inflation does to the aggregate price level each year.

options_template.text: Cooling inflation from 8% to 3% was disinflation, not deflation: average consumer prices continued rising at 3% per year atop the elevated post-2022 price plateau.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Disinflation slows the speed at which prices climb but does not reverse prior price-level increases; returning to 2019 prices would require sustained deflation (pi < 0).

options_template.text: The CPI measures only producer wholesale prices and fails to capture retail rent and grocery bills.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (CPI Scope): Housing/rent and groceries are core components of the urban consumer CPI basket.

options_template.text: Disinflation means prices fell by 5% each year, so household frustration must reflect money illusion.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Confusing Disinflation with Deflation): Falling from 8% to 3% inflation means prices rose 3%, not that prices fell 5%.

options_template.text: Because nominal wages automatically drop during disinflation, prices appear higher even when they actually fell.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Disinflation Dynamics): Prices did not fall during 2023–2024 U.S. disinflation, and nominal wages do not automatically decline when inflation cools.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Japan's Lost Decades of Deflation and Spending Delays
questions.title: Japan's Lost Decades of Deflation and Spending Delays
questions.prompt_template: Following the burst of its asset-price bubble in the early 1990s, Japan experienced prolonged deflation (pi_t < 0) across much of the late 1990s and 2000s. Why did expectations of continuing deflation weaken Japanese household consumption and business investment?

hints.text: Think about what a rational shopper or firm does when they expect cars, appliances, and equipment to be cheaper next year.
Consider also how falling prices affect the real burden of existing fixed-dollar debts.

options_template.text: Expecting prices to be even lower next year encouraged households to postpone durable purchases and corporations to delay capital investment, while rising real debt burdens depressed spending further.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Expected deflation creates a powerful incentive to wait for lower future prices and increases the real burden of nominal debt (debt deflation), reinforcing economic stagnation.

options_template.text: Deflation caused severe shoe-leather costs as Japanese households rushed to spend physical cash before it lost purchasing power.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Inflation vs. Deflation Incentives): Rushing to spend cash before it loses value occurs during high inflation, whereas deflation increases the real value of holding cash.

options_template.text: Deflation reduced the real interest rate on fixed-rate corporate loans below zero, discouraging banks from collecting payments.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Deflation and Real Rates): Because r = i - pi, negative inflation (pi < 0) pushes the real interest rate above the nominal rate (r > i), raising real borrowing costs.

options_template.text: Deflation caused rapid tax bracket creep that pushed Japanese workers into higher marginal income tax brackets.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Bracket Creep Direction): Bracket creep is caused by rising nominal incomes during inflation, not by falling prices during deflation.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Real Purchasing-Power Erosion of an Unindexed Minimum Wage
questions.title: Real Purchasing-Power Erosion of an Unindexed Minimum Wage
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a statutory federal minimum wage remains fixed at $7.25 per hour in nominal terms for fifteen consecutive years while the Consumer Price Index rises every year. How does the real purchasing power of that statutory wage floor evolve over those fifteen years?

hints.text: Inspect W_real = ($7.25 / CPI_t) * 100 as CPI_t grows year after year.
Compare an unindexed statutory wage floor with an indexed benefit such as Social Security.

options_template.text: Its real purchasing power declines steadily every single year because the fixed $7.25 nominal wage is divided by a continuously rising CPI.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without automatic CPI indexation, positive inflation steadily erodes the real goods and services that a fixed nominal minimum wage can purchase.

options_template.text: Its real purchasing power stays constant because $7.25 per hour is written into federal law.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Nominal vs. Real Rigidity): Statutory law fixes the nominal dollar figure ($7.25), not the real basket of goods it buys.

options_template.text: Its real purchasing power rises automatically whenever the economy experiences disinflation.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Disinflation Still Erodes Fixed Wages): During disinflation, prices are still rising (pi > 0), so a fixed nominal wage continues losing real purchasing power, just more slowly.

options_template.text: Its real purchasing power rises by 0.5 to 1.0 percentage points per year due to CPI substitution bias.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Bias vs. Indexation): CPI upward bias affects indexed contracts (like COLAs), not an unindexed $7.25 wage that receives no CPI adjustment at all.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Capital Gains Taxes on Illusory Nominal Gains
questions.title: Capital Gains Taxes on Illusory Nominal Gains
questions.prompt_template: An investor buys shares of a stock for $10,000 and sells them one year later for $11,000 (+10.0% nominal return) during a year when CPI inflation is exactly 10.0%. If the tax code levies a 20% capital gains tax on the $1,000 nominal gain ($200 tax), what is the investor's true real after-tax outcome?

hints.text: First determine the investor's pre-tax real gain when both the asset price and consumer prices rose 10.0%.
Then consider the effect of paying $200 in taxes on that zero pre-tax real gain.

options_template.text: The investor earned zero real pre-tax gain, so paying $200 in tax on the illusory nominal gain leaves the investor with a negative real after-tax return—a textbook unit-of-account cost of inflation.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $11,000 buys the exact same basket of goods as $10,000 did a year earlier, taxing the $1,000 nominal gain leaves the investor with $10,800—less real purchasing power than they started with.
