options_template.text: The investor earned a +8.0% real after-tax return because $800 of the $1,000 profit remained after taxes.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Money Illusion in Investing): $800 is the nominal after-tax dollar increase; once adjusted for 10.0% inflation, $10,800 buys less than $10,000 did a year earlier.

options_template.text: The investor broke even in real terms because capital gains taxes are automatically refunded when inflation matches nominal returns.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Unindexed Capital Gains): U.S. capital gains taxes are assessed on nominal dollar gains rather than inflation-adjusted real gains.

options_template.text: This scenario illustrates shoe-leather costs because the investor had to sell stock to pay taxes.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Unit-of-Account vs. Shoe-Leather Costs): Taxing illusory nominal gains because the dollar yardstick shrank is a unit-of-account cost, not a shoe-leather cost.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Domestic Capital Goods Price Surge: GDP Deflator vs. CPI
questions.title: Domestic Capital Goods Price Surge: GDP Deflator vs. CPI
questions.prompt_template: Suppose prices of domestically manufactured commercial airplanes and industrial factory machinery surge by 18%, while prices of all household consumer goods and services remain completely unchanged. How will the U.S. GDP Implicit Price Deflator and the U.S. CPI (CPIAUCSL) respond?

hints.text: Identify which GDP expenditure component (C, I, G, or X) includes commercial airplanes and industrial machinery.
Ask whether typical urban households buy commercial airliners or factory machinery in their retail market basket.

options_template.text: The GDP Implicit Price Deflator rises because domestically produced business investment goods (I) are part of GDP, whereas the CPI stays unchanged because households do not purchase commercial airplanes or factory machinery.
options_template.feedback: Correct. The GDP Deflator covers all domestic final output (C, I, G, X), including business investment goods, whereas the CPI tracks only urban consumer retail purchases.

options_template.text: The CPI rises sharply while the GDP Deflator stays unchanged because industrial goods carry heavy fixed weights in the CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Reversed Index Scope): Commercial capital equipment belongs to investment (I) in the GDP Deflator, not to the urban consumer basket.

options_template.text: Both the GDP Deflator and the CPI stay unchanged because capital machinery is treated as an intermediate good excluded from GDP.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Final Investment vs. Intermediate Goods): Newly produced capital equipment and commercial aircraft are final investment goods (I) included in GDP and its deflator.

options_template.text: Both indexes rise by the exact same 18% because every domestic price change passes identically into both indexes.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Identical Weights): The two indexes differ in scope and weighting, so pure capital-goods price shocks move the GDP Deflator without directly moving the CPI.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: The Fisher Effect on Newly Issued Bonds vs. Existing Fixed-Rate Bonds
questions.title: The Fisher Effect on Newly Issued Bonds vs. Existing Fixed-Rate Bonds
questions.prompt_template: Suppose lenders and borrowers require an expected real interest rate of r^e = 3.0%, and expected annual inflation suddenly rises from pi^e = 2.0% to pi^e = 5.0%. According to the Fisher Effect, how does this shift affect the nominal interest rate on newly issued loans compared with existing fixed-rate loans?

hints.text: Use i = r^e + pi^e to compute the nominal rate on newly issued loans before and after expected inflation rises.
Distinguish between new loan contracts negotiated today and old fixed-rate contracts signed in the past.

options_template.text: Nominal interest rates on newly issued loans rise one-for-one from 5.0% to 8.0%, whereas existing fixed-rate loans remain locked at their original 5.0% nominal rate.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under the Fisher Effect, higher expected inflation (+3.0 percentage points) pushes new nominal rates up one-for-one (from 5.0% to 8.0%) to preserve r^e = 3.0%, while previously signed fixed-rate contracts cannot adjust.

options_template.text: Nominal interest rates on both newly issued loans and all existing fixed-rate loans automatically jump to 8.0%.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ex-Ante vs. Ex-Post Adjustment): Existing fixed-rate loans have legally locked nominal rates; only newly issued contracts incorporate the new inflation expectations.

options_template.text: Nominal interest rates on newly issued loans stay at 5.0%, forcing the expected real return on new loans down to 0.0% permanently.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Ignoring the Fisher Effect): Lenders will not voluntarily issue new loans at 0% expected real return when they require 3.0%; they demand a higher nominal rate.

options_template.text: Nominal interest rates on newly issued loans fall from 5.0% to 2.0% because higher inflation reduces the value of money.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Sign of Fisher Effect): Higher expected inflation raises—not lowers—nominal interest rates so lenders are compensated for expected purchasing-power erosion.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Policy Trade-Offs of Switching from Standard CPI to Chained CPI
questions.title: Policy Trade-Offs of Switching from Standard CPI to Chained CPI
questions.prompt_template: Policymakers have periodically debated switching federal benefit COLAs from the standard fixed-weight CPI to the Chained CPI (SUUR0000SA0). Which statement accurately evaluates the economic and fiscal consequences of that switch?

hints.text: Recall how the Chained CPI reduces upward substitution bias relative to the standard Laspeyres CPI.
Trace what slightly smaller annual percentage adjustments mean for federal budget outlays and constant-utility measurement.

options_template.text: Because the Chained CPI accounts for consumer substitution and grows slightly more slowly than the standard CPI, switching reduces long-run federal benefit outlays while tracking true constant-utility living costs more accurately.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Accounting for substitution lowers measured inflation slightly compared to a fixed-weight Laspeyres index, reducing long-run federal COLA spending while aligning adjustments closer to true cost-of-living changes.

options_template.text: Switching to the Chained CPI would raise federal benefit outlays sharply because Chained CPI grows faster than the standard Laspeyres CPI.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Direction of Substitution Bias): Because consumers substitute away from items whose prices rise fastest, Chained CPI grows slightly more slowly—not faster—than the standard fixed-weight CPI.

options_template.text: Switching to the Chained CPI would eliminate all inflation in the U.S. economy by preventing businesses from raising prices.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Measurement vs. Price Setting): Changing the statistical index formula improves cost-of-living measurement; it does not directly control firm pricing behavior.

options_template.text: Switching to the Chained CPI would exclude imported consumer goods from benefit calculations because the Chained CPI is identical to the GDP Deflator.
options_template.feedback: Misconception (Chained CPI vs. GDP Deflator): The Chained CPI still tracks urban consumer purchases (including imports), unlike the GDP Deflator.
